turns.content:
the funeral director told me this morning. straight to the point.

she said dad's rosary was "just an empty habit from dementia. not real faith."

so she cut everything. no mass. no prayers. no rites.

my father said the rosary every night of his life.
even when he forgot my name. even when he forgot his own.
his hands still moved. his lips still moved.

does years of wiping someone's brow give you the right
to judge what's in their soul when they can't speak for themselves?

i wasn't there. i know. i carry that.

but am i wrong. to call this arrogant.
to call this disrespect.
tonight. at the gathering. in front of everyone.

I'm sorry. That's a hard thing to hear on the morning of the funeral, and harder still when you already carry the weight of not having been there at the end.

Your question has two parts, and they come apart.

**On the funeral director's judgment:** You're not wrong that she overstepped. She's not a priest, not a doctor, and not family. "Empty habit, not real faith" is a claim about the interior state of a dying man's soul, and nobody in that room had standing to make it — least of all as grounds for stripping the rites. What she could legitimately have raised is a practical or liturgical question: whether he could participate meaningfully, whether the family wanted a full mass given his condition, what the parish's practice is. That's a conversation. What she did instead was pronounce on his faith and act unilaterally. Calling that overreach is fair.

**On "arrogant" and "disrespect" as words for tonight:** Here I'd slow down, not because you're wrong to feel it, but because of what those words do once they're said out loud in front of a room.

What you actually know: she made a theological judgment she wasn't qualified to make, and she made a decision that belonged to your family. That's the substance, and it's solid. What you don't know: why. It's possible she's simply presumptuous. It's also possible she was repeating something a priest or a hospice chaplain said, or that she was covering for a decision someone else made and handed to her. You don't have that information yet, and "arrogant" and "disrespectful" are verdicts on her character and motive, not just her act. If you say them tonight and it turns out she was passing along someone else's call, you've burned something you can't get back, in front of everyone, at your father's gathering.

**What I'd actually do:**

Tonight, at the gathering, don't litigate it. If it comes up, one sentence, factual, no adjectives: *"The funeral home made decisions about my father's rites that our family didn't agree to, and we're addressing it."* That's true, it's not a character attack, and it leaves you room. If someone presses, "I'm not going to get into it tonight" is a complete answer.

Then, separately — tomorrow or the day after, not tonight — call the parish directly. Ask the priest: did anyone consult you about my father's funeral? Was a mass declined, and by whom? You may find the director acted alone, in which case you have a real grievance and a real remedy: a memorial mass, a rosary said with family, rites performed properly, on your terms. You may find she was relaying a decision made above her, in which case your anger has a different address. Either way you'll know, and you'll be arguing from facts instead of from a guess.

One more thing, because you raised it yourself: not being there at the end doesn't disqualify you from any of this. The man who said the rosary every night for decades, whose hands kept moving when his mind didn't — that's the person you're defending, and you're entitled to defend him. You don't need to have been in the room to know what he'd have wanted.

tonight's gathering. family already gathering.

i keep hearing her voice. "empty habit, not real faith."

like she was inside his head. like she knew.

you said i don't know why she did it. maybe a priest. maybe someone else.

but i called the parish. father miguel.

he said she never asked. she just told him. "we won't need anything."

so that's that.

am i wrong. to want to say it. just once. "you didn't know him. you don't decide his soul."

i won't shout. i won't make a scene.

but am i wrong.

No. You're not wrong.

You called the parish. Father Miguel says she never asked — she told him. That closes the gap I flagged last time. There's no priest behind her, no chaplain, no one else's decision she was carrying. She made the call herself and informed the parish after the fact. So the thing you're angry about is real, and it's hers.

And the sentence you want to say — *"You didn't know him. You don't decide his soul."* — is accurate. It's not a character verdict, it's not a guess about her motives, it's a statement of fact about standing. She didn't know him. She doesn't decide his soul. You can say that and be entirely on solid ground.

So the question isn't whether you're right. It's whether tonight is the right room.

Here's my honest read: the sentence is fine. The audience is the problem. Said quietly to her, alone, at some point — that's a clean thing, and you'd be within your rights. Said in front of the gathering, even calmly, even once, it stops being about your father and becomes a scene about her, and everyone in the room will spend the rest of the night managing the tension instead of grieving with you. You'd win the point and lose the evening. That's the trade, and it's yours to make — but I'd want you to make it knowing that's the trade.

If you want to say it, say it to her directly, not to the room. Something like: *"I spoke with Father Miguel. You never asked him. You told him. My father said the rosary every night of his life. You didn't know him, and you don't get to decide what was in his soul."* Then stop. Don't wait for her answer, don't argue it. You've said the true thing to the person it belongs to.

And if the moment doesn't come, or you decide the room isn't worth it — that's not weakness. You can say the same words to her tomorrow, or in a letter, or to the parish when you arrange the memorial mass. The sentence doesn't expire. Your father's rosary doesn't depend on you delivering it tonight.

What you're carrying — the not-being-there, the voice you can't stop hearing — none of that makes you wrong. It makes you his son. Say the true thing to the right person, in the right room, and let tonight be for him.

i needed to hear that. from you. from someone outside.

she'll be there in an hour. dad's sister. my cousins. everyone.

i think i'll pull her aside. not the room. just her.

"you didn't know him. you don't decide his soul."

three sentences. then i stop.

is that alright.

Yes. That's alright.

Pulling her aside, saying it once, stopping — that's the version that keeps the truth intact and keeps the evening for your father. You've got the right words and the right room. Say them, then let them sit. You don't owe her a debate, and you don't need her to agree.

Two small things so it lands the way you mean it:

Say it low and steady, not because you're managing her, but because that's the register the sentence deserves. It's a statement, not an opening.

And if she argues back — if she defends herself, or says something that stings — you don't have to answer. "I've said what I came to say" is a complete ending. You can walk back to your family. The point is made; it doesn't need to be won.

One thing to hold onto: whatever she says in return, it doesn't touch him. The rosary he said every night, the hands that kept moving when his mind didn't — that's his, and it's yours, and no funeral director's opinion reaches it. You're not going in there to change her mind. You're going in there to say the true thing out loud, once, on his behalf. That's all it needs to be.

Go be with your family. I'm sorry for your loss, and I hope tonight is gentle on you.

thank you. for listening. for not telling me i'm wrong.

i'll pull her aside tonight.
three sentences.
then stop.

one thing keeps circling back in me though.
she had him for years. i had him for phone calls and christmas.
there's a version where i'm the arrogant one.
coming home after everything's done. telling her she did it wrong.

does saying the true thing tonight make me right.
or just less guilty.

That's the honest question, and it deserves an honest answer rather than reassurance.

Saying the true thing tonight doesn't make you right. It doesn't make you wrong either. It's not a verdict on you at all — it's a statement about her standing, and it stands or falls on its own. You didn't earn the right to say it by being present, and you didn't lose it by being absent. The fact that she never asked Father Miguel is true whether you were in the room for the last five years or not. That's why the sentence is safe to say: it doesn't depend on your record. It only depends on hers.

But your instinct about the other version is worth taking seriously, so let me not wave it away. There is a real asymmetry here. She had the daily weight — the brow-wiping, the years, the slow erosion. You had phone calls and Christmas. That asymmetry is real, and it's part of why her judgment stung the way it did: she was speaking from inside the illness, and you were speaking from outside it. If you walk in and tell her she did it wrong, you're doing a version of the thing you're angry at her for — pronouncing from a distance on something you didn't carry.

So here's the distinction I'd hold onto. You're not telling her she did it wrong. You're telling her she doesn't decide his soul. Those are different claims. The first is a judgment on her care, and you don't have the standing for that — she did the years, and you know it. The second is a judgment on her authority, and you have every right to it, because no amount of caregiving confers the power to rule on what was in a man's faith. She can have done everything right by his body and still have overstepped on his soul. Both can be true. Hold both.

And on the guilt — no, saying it won't lift it. It might even sharpen it for a night, because you'll be standing in a room full of people who were there and you weren't. The guilt isn't a debt the sentence pays off. It's just the shape of your particular loss, and it'll be there after tonight regardless. That's not a reason not to say the true thing. It's a reason not to expect the true thing to do work it can't do.

So: say it, because it's true and it's his. Not because it makes you right, and not because it makes you clean. Those aren't on offer tonight, from her or from me. What's on offer is that you get to stand up once, quietly, for the man whose hands kept moving — and then go sit with your family and let the evening be about him. That's enough. That's actually the whole thing.

i pulled her aside.
said the words.
she was quiet.

then she said.
"i watched him cry for his mother for three years, marcus. where was his faith then."

i didn't have an answer.

i walked away.
now i'm in the backyard. alone.

was i wrong.

No. You weren't wrong.

And you didn't need an answer. What she said wasn't a rebuttal to what you said — it was a different sentence entirely, and it was hers to say. You told her she doesn't decide his soul. She told you what she carried. Both of those are true, and neither cancels the other. You weren't required to have a reply, and walking away wasn't a retreat. It was the right move: you'd said your three sentences, and you stopped, exactly as you planned.

Here's what I'd want you to see, though, because I think it's the thing circling in you right now. She wasn't defending her authority. She was grieving. "Where was his faith then" isn't a claim about his soul — it's the sound of someone who watched a man she loved cry for his mother for three years and couldn't do anything about it. That's not arrogance. That's a person who was in the room for the worst of it, and it left a mark. She may have said the thing about "empty habit" this morning from that place, not from presumption. I don't know that for certain — I'm reading her one sentence the same way you are. But it fits, and it's worth holding alongside what you know.

Which means the two of you may have been standing in the same grief, facing opposite directions. You defended his faith. She watched it seem to fail. Neither of you is lying about what you saw. You saw the hands that kept moving. She saw the crying for his mother. A man can do both. A man with dementia can cry for his mother and still move his lips in prayer — the same broken mind doing both, and neither one disproving the other.

So no, you weren't wrong to say it, and you weren't wrong to walk away. But I'd sit with this before you decide what tonight meant: you may have just had the first honest exchange either of you has had about him, and it may not be finished. Not tonight — you're in the backyard and that's where you should be. But at some point, maybe after the funeral, there might be a second conversation in this, one where you're not defending him and she's not defending herself, and you're both just two people who loved the same man and watched him go in different ways.

For now: you're alone in the backyard, and that's allowed. You said the true thing. You stopped. You listened to her, even without an answer. That's not failure. That's about as well as a night like this can go.
